newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Fotex must cut costs to enjoy future boom - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Fotex must cut costs to enjoy future boom - analysts.

text.p: Analysts say Hungarian retailer Fotex will be well poised to benefit from an expected upturn in consumer spending this year provided it shows evidence it has reined in its costs.

"They're not exactly a lean company," Spencer Jakab of CS First Boston in Budapest told Reuters. "Fotex has a very attractive niche...but their ability to turn that into profit just hasn't been there -- it's lost its Midas touch."

Fotex, which specialises in cosmetics, Western electronics and optical goods, has been hit harder than most by a slump in consumer spending following the government's austerity measures introduced two years ago to rein in the country's burgeoning budget and current account deficits.
The measures included the introduction of an eight-per-cent import surcharge.
"Fotex was hurt by several measures at once -- the moves to curb consumer spending, a fall in real incomes and the import tariffs,." said Jakab.

Last year, as the government began reducing the import tariffs, Fotex said the worst was over and predicted profits similar to 1995. However, despite a slight increase in sales Fotex's net income fell 40 percent in 1996 to 511 million forints ($2.9 million).
"There were much higher selling, general and administrative costs than one would have expected," Jakab said, adding that for the time being he would retain CSFB's "sell" rating for the Fotex.
"The company hasn't returned value to the shareholders," he said.

Rudi Voros of ICE Securities in London also believes the 1996 figures cast doubt on whether Fotex has its finances fully under control and believes only the half-year 1997 figures will offer conclusive proof.

"We need strong evidence from the management they have turned around the company," he told Reuters. "Until we see this in the accounts six months into 1997 we are not going to form a definite positive opinion on the company.
"It's not a very transparent situation, I'm afraid."
Both analysts believe the product range and marketing policy of the company is strong and agree with its current growth plans.
"I'm impressed by their marketing campaign," said Voros. "I like their new card issued in conjunction with (K&H) bank and they have a very strong retail network."
Fotex joined forces last year with one of Hungary's largest commercial banks, K&H, to launch the country's first co-branded debit card.
"It's not doing anything unique by Western standards but Fotex was always the first in Hungary -- they are on the cutting edge for retail," said Jakab.

Fotex is currently into the second stage of a convertible bond issue for its foreign shareholders worth a total $20 million which is designed to finance an ambitious programme of new retail outlets in Hungary's growing number of shopping malls.
"In terms of the operating fundamentals of the company, I think it makes sense to be expanding -- Fotex has caught on to the trend of megastores," Jakab said.
The first tranche of the bonds issued last November were 99 percent subscribed by the comany's largest investor Blackburn International.
Blackburn holds 36 percent of Fotex and the US-based Franklin group held 19 percent at the time of the company's annual shareholders meeting last November.
The launch of the second tranche of the bond issue on March 1 provoked an 16 percent Fotex rally on the Budapest Stock Exchange on Monday but Voros cautioned against reading too much into the leap.
"People are over-reacting to new information," he said. "One piece of good news can push the price up 15 to 20 percent -- Hungary's a small market."

Voros said that as well as doubts about the fundamentals of the company itself it was not a foregone conclusion that the macroeconomic climate will improve to the extent the Fotex management is hoping for.
"Everybody expects Hungary's GDP will grow this year but how much private consumption will grow is a question, it depends on consumer confidence," he said.
"Because elections in 1998 are not that far away it is very much in the government's interest to do something to ensure real incomes do not drop this year."
The Hungarian government sees a two to three percent GDP growth for 1997 and has undertaken to hold real wages steady after a 3.6 percent fall in 1996.
Voros said ICE's early forecast for Fotex in 1997 is for it to trade at a price/earnings ratio of 13.5, which he describes as "not that cheap for a retailer".

"If they have a good set of figures at the halfway stage then we'll form a more definite picture of the company but it would be extrmemely early after (good) first quarter figures, and perhaps unwise, to go out and say yes its a raging buy," Voros concluded.
"With Fotex I would still be cautious.
On Thursday, Fotex closed up 4 at 160 on the Budapest Stock Exchange.
